Use the separable–purely inseparable decomposition in characteristic exponent \(q\).

First prove the standard characterization
\[
x\in F^{\mathrm{perf}}\subseteq E
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{sepdeg}(\minpoly_F(x))=1.
\]
Indeed, separable degree \(1\) means that the minimal polynomial is purely inseparable; equivalently, for some \(n\),
\[
x^{q^n}\in F.
\]
This remains valid when \(E\) is only a domain by passing to its fraction field and observing that membership in the range of the algebra map has the stated ring-theoretic meaning.

For the second conjunct, organize both sides around the same mechanism:

- Establish the elementwise lemma: if \(x/F\) is separable, then
  \[
  F(x)=F(x^q).
  \]
  The extension \(F(x)/F(x^q)\) is purely inseparable, but it lies inside the separable extension \(F(x)/F\); hence it must be trivial.

- Apply this to every \(s\in S\). The assumed separability of \(F(S)/F\) makes each \(s\) separable, so \(s\in F(S^q)\), yielding
  \[
  F(S)\subseteq F(S^q).
  \]
  The reverse inclusion is immediate.

- Identify the domain-side assertion with the purely inseparable criterion above: separable degree \(1\) is equivalent to \(x^{q^n}\) lying in the image of \(F\) for some \(n\).

Thus the adjoin equality and the power-in-the-base characterization are two formulations of the fact that an extension cannot be simultaneously nontrivially separable and purely inseparable. The essential assumption is separability of \(F(S)/F\); without it, adjoining \(q\)-th powers can genuinely produce a smaller field.
